newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals--Molybdenum tight on growing demand.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals--Molybdenum tight on growing demand.

text.p: Japan's molybdenum spot market remained tight as the weaker yen spurred demand from export oriented industries, traders said on Tuesday.
"Supplies are tight. The price is likely to go up again," said one trader at a major trade house. "We've seen a weak yen, and exporters are faring well," he said.
Traders said the spot price of molybdenum, mainly used for stainless steel production, stood at around $4.60-4.70 per lb, only slightly below the recent peak of $4.80 last month.
Many expect spot molybdenum prices to cling to the high price levels before softening in July when Molycorp of the United States is expected to begin shipping material after months of delay.

Traders said Japan was likely to see healthy growth in demand this year against the backdrop of a lower yen, which has helped stainless steel product makers, such as pipe and automobile makers, gain international competitiveness.
"We are bullish this year. The (molybdenum) price will rise a little further. It might exceed $5.00," said another trader, who predicts domestic demand to expand by more than five percent this year.
The latest official statistics show molybdenum demand in Japan, which accounts for about 15 percent of global demand, totalled 6,961 tonnes in 1995. Official data for 1996 was not yet available.
Yet as far as the long-term price is concerned, not many are bullish, with some forecasting a decline to $3.50 if Molycorp resumes production without any hitches.
A trader in Beijing said he was able to source Chinese molybdenum oxide for prompt shipment at $4.30/4.50.
However, he said Japanese buyers were seeking steeper discounts and were taking only small parcels.

In the cobalt market, prices remained strong as rebel forces in Zaire, the world's largest cobalt producer, moved towards Kinshasa after their leader Laurent Kabila failed to reach an agreement with President Mobutu Sese Seko on Sunday.
Traders said high grade cobalt was quoted at $25.50 per lb and Russian grade at $23-24 on Tuesday when many Japanese players returned from the "Golden Week" holiday.
"We'll start to see some kind of movement in the market later this week," said one trader, who added he had heard some U.S. users purchased the metal for $25.50 late last week.

Traders said U.S. users, although hit by the suspension of U.S. stockpile cobalt sales due to a legal dispute between the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA) and Minor Metals Inc, have been waiting for prices to ease before buying.

Some traders speculated that U.S. users would buy cobalt in the market, after the DLA failed to sell about 500 tonnes in March. Some traders doubted the DLA's sales of about 500 tonnes in February had gone through as reported.
One trader brushed aside bullish market views saying: "I can't imagine the price staying so high. Japanese main users remain cool."
A number of traders in China and Hong Kong were occupied with bismuth, citing good demand in the pharmaceutical industries of Europe, Japan and the United States.
Business had already been done at $3.45 lb cif Baltimore, and at $3.55 c&f (cost and freight) Japan, a Hong Kong trader said, adding that he was now hearing Chinese offers at $3.55/60.
Indium prices have moved up over the past two to three months, a trader said, making further rises above $300 per kg difficult.
"Even if we offer $260 kg, no one will buy," he said. "So I think traders and consumers expect the market to drop, and they are waiting to see," the trader said.
-- Lynne O'Donnell, Shanghai newsroom (86-21) 6279-8544 -- Nao Nakanishi, Tokyo Commodities +81-3 3432 6179
